abstract: Low selectivity is one of the greatest challenges of an electrocatalytic CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR), e.g., using copper-based catalysts in water solution. Herein, we report the production of pure acetate (aside from H2) from a CO2RR with a novel polymeric Cu–ligand (pyridinic N and carbonyl group) complex (p-CuL) core–shell microsphere synthesized by a facile thermal-polymerization of urea and a Cu–urea complex. The highly selective reduction of CO2 to acetate, without any detectable gas products besides H2, is enabled by the unique co-coordination of pyridinic N and CvO with copper whose chemical state is between +1 and +2 and the porous 3D core that is kinetically favorable for the acetate product. The maximal faradaic efficiency of acetate of ∼64% is attained at −0.37 V vs. RHE in a 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte, and H2 evolution is much suppressed. In the process of the CO2RR to acetate, the Cu (II)–carbonyl coordination remains while Cu–ligand active sites are reduced to Cu(I). In addition, the highly selective acetate production is favored by the p-CuL core–shell microsphere for the adsorption of some important intermediates of CO2 reduction and their dimerization and further e /h reduction, as seen from the distinctly increased CvO and –OH groups in the O K-edge X-ray absorption spectrum (XAS) of p-CuL after the CO2RR.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The massive carbon dioxide emission from the burning of traditional fossil fuels has contributed to serious environmental problems and global warming.1 It has been regarded as a promising and sustainable developmental strategy to upgrade CO2 to hydrocarbon fuel and high-value chemicals utilizing renewable electrical energy.2–4 In the past decades, tremendous efforts and great progress have been made to develop electrocatalysts for the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) towards high productivity and high selectivity.5 Effective deepreduction of CO2 to C2+ products in water solution has been reported using many catalysts, among which copper-based materials have been considered some of the most promising electrocatalysts.6,7 However, it remains a big challenge to
achieve high efficiency and selectivity. Currently, poor selectivity, high overpotential and/or severely competitive HERs have been commonly observed, which significantly limit the industrial application of CO2RRs. 8
A CO2RR involves a highly complex multi-electron/proton transfer process and generally results in the coexistence of a range of reduction products such as CO, CH4, ethylene, HCOOH, alcohols, oxalic acid, etc. Although highly challenging, it is highly desirable to achieve the highly selective CO2RR to obtain targeted high-valued C2+ products. It has been suggested that the CO2RR efficiency and product selectivity are dependent on various types of product-specific active sites that feature different adsorption energies of the *COOH intermediate during CO2 reduction on oxide-derived Cu catalysts, as reported in the study of Lum and co-workers.9 A highly selective CO2RR towards specific C1 or C2+ products at a less-negative potential has been attempted using various copper complexes, such as an oxalate product on a dinuclear copper(I) complex,10 CO on a copper(I) boryl complex11 and CH4 on a copper(II) phthalocyanine complex.
12 The high selectivity of various catalysts for a CO2RR has been thought to be highly related to the local environment of active sites,13 an appropriate adsorption strength of key intermediates,14–16 and the nature of the coordinated ligand in metalcomplexes.17 †Electronic supplementary information (ESI) available: The XRD pattern of the resultant p-CuL, FE-SEM graphs of p-CuL-6 and p-CuL-8, electrochemical Double Layer Capacitance (DLC) diagram of p-CuL, Jacetate normalized to the ESCA diagram. Acetate, an important industrial compound is considerably difficult to achieve as an 8e− reduction product of the CO2RR due to high energy barriers for C–C coupling. Electrocatalytic CO2RRs to acetate have been reported on a few copper-based catalysts but with low selectivity and faradaic efficiency and at a relatively high overpotential. For example, a mixture of acetate (208.7 µmol h−1 gCu −1), HCOOH (212.7 µmol h−1 gCu −1) and methanol (13.6 µmol h−1 gCu −1) has been demonstrated on Cu nanoparticles deposited on CNTs (Cu/CNTs) at −1.4 V vs. Ag/AgCl,18 a mixture of CH3COOH (16.8%) and HCOOH (68.4%) has been demonstrated on copper porphyrin metal– organic framework nanosheets at −1.55 V vs. Ag/Ag+,19 and a mixture of acetate (21.2%), HCOOH, CO and CH4 has been demonstrated on ultrasmall (Cu)n(Ag)m bimetallic nanoparticles at −1.33 V vs. the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE).20 Nevertheless, pure acetate generation besides H2 has never been reported on a copper complex.
Herein, we report a novel polymeric Cu–ligand (p-CuL) complex core–shell microsphere, showing a highly selective CO2RR to acetate at a low potential, benefitting from its unique local chemical environment of Cu–ligand coordination and the porous inner framework. This p-CuL complex is formed with the coordinated ligands of pyridinic N and carbonyl moieties and the chemical state of Cuδ+ is between +1 and +2. Its preparation and properties and the CO2 reduction performance have been investigated in detail, along with the change in the copper oxidation state, Cu–ligand coordination environment and surface oxygen-bearing groups before and after the CO2RR, and the possible mechanism. As only pure acetate is formed besides H2 for the electrochemical CO2RR with the novel p-CuL catalyst as reported in this work, we hope that this work can provide some new insights and inspire more exciting findings and discoveries in the electrochemical CO2RR in the future.

sections.heading: 2.1. Synthesis of the p-CuL catalyst
sections.text:

Then the mixture was transferred to a Teflon-lined stainless steel autoclave and maintained at 180 °C for 4–8 h. After cooling to room temperature, a blue and sticky solid was collected and washed with deionized water until a purple sediment was obtained, which was dried under vacuum at 50 °C overnight. The sample was named p-CuL-t, where t was the reaction time. In this paper, unless otherwise stated, the p-CuL discussed below was obtained after a 4 h reaction at 180 °C.
Cu–urea complex. The Cu–urea complex precursor was prepared using a modified method reported in the literature.21 Typically, 25.0 mmol copper nitrate trihydrate and 85.0 mmol urea were dissolved in 100.0 mL of a hot absolute ethanol solution (60 °C) under stirring. A blue precipitate quickly settled at the bottom of the flask. This precipitate was collected by centrifugation and then dried under vacuum at 60 °C overnight for the preparation of the p-CuL catalyst.

sections.heading: 2.2. Physicochemical characterization
sections.text: The crystallinity of p-CuL was studied by X-ray powder diffraction (XRD) on a Bruker D8 advance diffractometer with Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.5405 Å) and a Lynxeye detector. The morphology was investigated using a high-resolution field-emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM, JSM-7100E, JEOL) and a transmission electron microscope (TEM, Tecnai G20, FEI, America). Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) and ultraviolet-visible (UV-Vis) spectra were collected on a NICOLET IS10 and a Shimadzu UV-2600 instrument, respectively. Elemental compositions and oxidation states were identified by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) (Kratos AXIS Ultra, Al Kα emission source) and Auger Cu LMM spectroscopy (Thermo Scientific NEXSA, Monochromatic Al Kα emission source). The surface chemical composition of the shell and the inner sphere was studied by XPS survey analyses before and after the sample was sputtered with 2 keV Ar+ ions for 250 seconds (Kratos AXIS Ultra, 2 keV Ar+ ion source). All signals were calibrated using the C 1s peak at 284.8 eV. The copper content was quantified by ICP-AES in a Thermo Scientific iCAP 6300 duo device. Soft X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS, the National Synchrotron Radiation Laboratory (NSRL), Hefei, China) was employed to probe the electronic structure, local coordination environment of copper sites and surface oxygenbearing species on p-CuL before and after the CO2RR.

sections.heading: 2.3. Electrochemical measurements
sections.text:
The electrochemical CO2RR was conducted on an H-type glass reaction system (150 mL) with a Nafion 117 membrane at ambient pressure and room temperature. All electrochemical responses were recorded on a CHI760E electrochemical workstation. A typical three-electrode cell configuration was used to investigate the CO2RR with platinum foil (15 × 15 × 0.2 mm) and Ag/AgCl electrodes (saturated KCl solution) as the counter and reference electrodes, respectively. The working electrode was prepared as follows. Typically, 10 mg of the catalyst was sonicated in 1.5 mL of isopropyl alcohol with 20 µL of a Nafion® perfluorinated resin solution (∼5% in a mixture of lower aliphatic alcohols and water) for 1 h to obtain an ink. Then, 30 μL of the ink was deposited on carbon paper (TGP-H-060) with an area of 1.0 cm2 (1.0 cm × 1.0 cm) and dried under vacuum at 50 °C overnight. The CO2RR was carried out under the following conditions. High purity CO2 (99.99%) was bubbled into 40 mL of 0.5 M KCHO3 electrolyte solution (pH = 7.2) in the cathode compartment at a flow rate of 5 mL min−1 for 30 minutes. The solution was magnetically stirred. All applied potentials were calibrated to the RHE using E (vs. RHE) = E (vs. Ag/AgCl) + 0.210 V + 0.0592 V × pH.
Gas products were identified on a gas chromatography instrument (GC, Zhejiang Fuli Analytical Instrument Co., Ltd, China) equipped with a flame ionization detector (FID) to detect CO, methane and hydrocarbons and a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) to detect H2. Ultrahigh purity N2 (99.99%) was used as the carrier gas. The quantification of gas products was carried out using calibration curves to standard gases.

Liquid products were quantified by 1H nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (NMR) (Bruker AVANCE III 400 MHz spectrometer) using dimethyl sulfoxide as an internal standard. The faradaic efficiencies (FEs) of acetate and H2 were calculated using the formula FE = nzF/Qtotal × 100%, where z is the number of transferred electrons (2 for H2 and 8 for acetate), n is the amount (mole) of the products, F is the Faraday constant (96 500 c mol−1) and Qtotal is the total amount of electrical charge. The partial current density of acetate ( jacetate) was calculated by multiplying FEacetate by the total current density.

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussion
sections.text:
Fig. 1A displays the synthesis process of water-insoluble purple p-CuL by the polymerization of Cu–urea and urea at 180 °C and the proposed molecular structure of p-CuL where the Cu ion is coordinated through nitrogen and carbonyl oxygen. In comparison, when only Cu–urea or urea was used, no product was obtained under the same reaction conditions. The XRD pattern of p-CuL (Fig. S1†) did not match with the characteristic peaks of any inorganic copper compounds such as metallic copper, copper oxides (CuO and Cu2O), Cu3N, etc., indicating that a new copper complex was likely formed. The FE-SEM graph in Fig. 1B shows an egg-like p-CuL microsphere with a size of about 1.2 μm. Interestingly, when the microsphere was bombarded with a higher-energy electron beam (15 keV), the surface was broken and the 3D porous core was exposed (Fig. 1C). The EDS elemental mapping images of the selected area featuring a 3D porous network displayed the uniform distribution of Cu, C, N and O elements, as shown in Fig. 1D. The TEM graph shown in Fig. 1E further confirmed the cross-linked porous structure of p-CuL.
To understand the copper–ligand coordination in the p-CuL complex, FT-IR spectra were recorded and are shown in
Fig. 2A. There was a remarkable change in the FTIR spectrum of the Cu–urea precursor compared with that of pure urea. The vibration frequency of the carbonyl group (CvO) shifted from 1680 cm−1 in urea (curve a) to a lower frequency of 1640 cm−1 in Cu–urea (curve b), and the –NH2 vibration slightly upshifted (Δv = 10 cm−1) to a higher frequency (3200–3450 cm−1). This suggested that copper was likely coordinated with oxygen in carbonyl groups (Cu–OvC) instead of nitrogen in –NH2 groups (process I in Fig. 1A), which was in accordance with the results of a previous report on the Cu– urea complex.21 After the polymerization of Cu–urea with urea (process II in Fig. 1A), the resulting p-CuL exhibited two new strong bands at 1678 and 1740 cm−1 from the CvO groups, besides the band at 1640 cm−1 from the carbonyl groups coordinated with copper. Meanwhile, the characteristic double peaks near 3350–3450 cm−1 of the primary amine (–NH2) in Cu–urea changed into one strong single peak at 3340 cm−1 from the secondary amine (–NH). These important changes indicated that imide (NH–CvO) groups were probably introduced into the p-CuL backbone. The additional new peaks in the range of 690–900 and 2800–3100 cm−1 were attributed to aromatic carbon rings. The strong vibrations at 1240–1610 cm−1 were attributed to the vibrations of CvN and C–N bonds in CN heterocycles.22 The bands at 427–457 and 550–590 cm−1 confirmed the coexistence of Cu–N and Cu–O coordination.23,24
The oxidation states of copper in p-CuL were investigated by CuLMM Auger electron emission spectroscopy and EPR spectroscopy. In the CuLMM Auger spectrum shown in Fig. 2B, the asymmetric broad peak located at ∼915 eV confirmed that the oxidation state of Cuδ+ in p-CuL was between Cu(I) and Cu(II),25 similar to the reported Cu–N–O bond in the Cu/polyimide complex26 and Cu(I)–TBA.27 Meanwhile, there was no observable Cu(0) peak (∼918 eV).25 The EPR spectrum in Fig. 2C shows a g value of 2.13 without observable hyperfine splitting

XPS analysis before and after Ar+ ion sputtering was employed to reveal the elemental composition in the surface shell and the inner 3D porous core in egg-like p-CuL microspheres, respectively. On the surface shell, the N 1s spectrum only showed a strong peak at 399.8 eV, likely ascribed to the imide groups (Fig. 2D, the curve before etching);29 the C 1s spectrum presented a strong peak at 289.2 eV and a weak band at 286.7 eV, attributed to the CvO and C–O bonds (Fig. 2E, the curve before etching),30,31 respectively. Those groups likely came from the incomplete condensation of Cu–urea/urea. In contrast, the inner porous skeleton (the curve after etching in Fig. 2D and E) features dramatically decreased imide groups, dominating pyridinic N (the strongest peak at 398.5 eV in Fig. 2D) and a small amount of pyrrolic N (400.7 eV);32,33 and markedly reduced carbonyl groups (CvO) at 289.2 eV along with the slightly enhanced C–O bond at 286.7 eV (Fig. 2E). The increase of pyridinic N and the significant decrease of the CvO groups indicated a deeper polymerization of Cu–urea and urea in the inner porous core.
UV-Vis DRS provided important information on the Cu– ligand coordination and geometric construction. p-CuL showed completely different absorption bands from the Cu– urea precursor. In Fig. 2F, the two strong absorption peaks near 230 and 278 nm were from metal–ligand charge transfer (MLCT)34 or π–π* transitions of aromatic rings.35 The well-separated and unsymmetric d–d transition bands in the visible light region with differentiable bands near 500 and 610 nm suggested that the copper ions bonded to sites with a low symmetry and formed a high-spin copper complex.36
The electrocatalytic activity of p-CuL for CO2 reduction was initially evaluated by linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) in a 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte solution. As shown in Fig. 3A, it was found that the polarization curve showed a steep increase of current density starting from −0.2 V (vs. RHE) under a CO2 atmosphere compared with that under an N2 atmosphere, indi-

cating that the p-CuL catalyst was electrocatalytically active for the CO2RR. Its electrochemical properties were further studied by cyclic voltammetry (CV) scanning from −0.3 to 1.3 V (vs. RHE). Prior to testing, the working electrode was activated through fast scanning at 500 mV s−1 for 50 cycles in 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte solution. As shown in Fig. 3B, a couple of peaks at Epa = 0.38 V (anodic) and Epc = 0.14 V (cathodic) under an N2 atmosphere were probably ascribed to the redox of Cu(II)/Cu(I). Under a CO2 atmosphere, the redox peaks became much more pronounced and showed a 90 mV positive shift of Epc. This indicated that CO2 was possibly involved in the redox reaction on p-CuL. In addition, the irreversible cathodic peak with a high current at −0.08 V was likely contributed by the CO2RR.
To investigate the electrocatalytic activity and quantify the product, the electrochemical CO2RR on p-CuL was conducted at different potentials ranging from −0.07 to −0.57 V vs. RHE. GC and 1H NMR spectroscopy were employed to detect the gas- and liquid-phase products, respectively. It was found that acetate was the only liquid product, and the H2 evolution reaction (HER) was the main competing reaction. There were no other products from CO2 reduction as detected by GC and
1H NMR. The faradaic efficiencies (FE) of the acetate and H2 products at various potentials were calculated and are shown in Fig. 3C. The initial acetate was detected at −0.07 V with a low FE of 3%. The competing HER was effectively suppressed at a relatively low potential (less negative than −0.37 V). The maximum FE of 64% was attained at −0.37 V at a rate of 150 μmol h−1 gcat−1. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time that Cu-based catalysts have shown such high productivity and selectivity in converting CO2 to acetate without any other detectable C1 or C2+ products (Table S1†).
However, at a more negative potential (<−0.37 V), H2 evolution dramatically increased and thus depressed the acetate production. Note that the total FE of acetate and H2 was lower than 100%. That could be due to the partial reduction of Cu(II) into Cu(I) during the CO2RR. This could be seen from the observed phenomenon that the current densities under various potentials decreased in the first 200 s and then became stable afterward (Fig. S2†), which indicated the possible initial surface Cu(II) reduction to Cu(I).
A series of controlled experiments were conducted to confirm the CO2RR on p-CuL and the data are presented in Table 1. The Cu–urea precursor was inactive towards the CO2RR, but p-CuL core–shell microspheres exhibited highly selective CO2RR activity to form acetate (FEacetate = 64%) in
0.5 M KHCO3 solution at −0.37 V, indicating that the acetate product was probably correlative with the local copper coordination environment in p-CuL. Moreover, the FEacetate in CO2 saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 was far higher than FEacetate of 8% in N2 saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 solution, indicating the low probability of direct HCO3
− reduction on p-CuL, and the following equilibrium between CO2 and HCO3 −:37,38

was crucial to obtaining high FEacetate. Furthermore, the CO2RR in the electrolyte without the involvement of HCO3 − was also investigated. In KH2PO4 solution (pH = 4.67), FEacetate of the CO2RR was 36%, while it was 29% in a KCl solution (pH = 7.27). This further illustrated that the equilibrium between CO2 and HCO3
− was highly related to the acetate product because the lower pH value promoted the right-shift of the equilibrium and increased the CO2 reactant on the electrode, thus resulting in a higher FEacetate in the KH2PO4 solution.
Furthermore, the pH effect of the electrolyte solution on the CO2RR was investigated by adjusting the concentration of KHCO3 and K2CO3 at an applied potential of −0.37 V vs. RHE. As shown in Fig. 3D, in a weakly acidic or neutral solution (pH = 6.18–7.18), the FEacetate gradually increased from 44 to 64% with the increasing pH value. However, in an alkaline solution (pH > 7.5), it kept dropping when the pH value continued to increase. This was probably ascribed to the fact that the increased HCO3
− concentration prompted the equilibrium HCO3
− + H+ ⇌ CO2 (reactant) + H2O to shift to the right side, thus providing much more CO2 reactant on the electrode in a weakly acidic or neutral solution, while the increasing pH in the alkaline region probably resulted from the increased CO3 2− species concentration, thus decreasing the CO2RR efficiency. From a kinetic viewpoint, a porous texture can achieve a better utilization of active sites and accelerate the mass transfer to boost catalytic activity.39 In this context, a series of p-CuL catalysts (p-CuL-t ) were prepared by simply changing the reaction time to control the polymerization of Cu–urea and urea. Elemental analysis and ICP-AES results demonstrated that various p-CuL-t catalysts retained almost the same atomic ratio of Cu : O : N : C (Table S2†) and copper content (∼21 wt%). However, FE-SEM graphs uncovered the distinctly different morphologies of p-CuL-t catalysts with different reaction times (Fig. 2A and Fig. S3†). As a result, in the applied potential range of 0 to −0.9 V vs. RHE, p-CuL-4 has the highest current density in the CO2 saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte solution among the three catalysts (Fig. 4A). Though the three p-CuL-t catalysts retained high selectivity for the acetate product, both FEacetate and the absolute yield of acetate were strongly dependent on the morphological structure of the catalyst. Under −0.37 V vs. RHE, FEacetate dramatically decreased in the order of p-CuL-4 (64%) > p-CuL-6 (42%) > p-CuL-8 (23%), as shown in Fig. 4B.
To probe the kinetics of the CO2RR on p-CuL catalysts, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was first carried out. Nonporous p-CuL-8 exhibited the largest electron transfer resistance (58.0 Ω),40 followed by the less dense p-CuL-6 (45.0 Ω) and the porous core–shell p-CuL-4 (30.3 Ω) (Fig. 4C). Furthermore, the electrochemical active surface area (ECSA) was evaluated by measuring the electrochemical double-layer capacitance (DLC) through repeating CV cycles in the potential range of 0.2–0.3 V vs. Ag/AgCl at a scanning rate ranging from 5 to 25 mV s−1 (Fig. S4†), where no faradaic process occurred. As shown in Fig. 4D, the DLC value determined by the slope of current density difference ( janode − jcathode) vs. scan rate plots was 42 mF cm−2 for p-CuL-4, twice and nine times as high as that of p-CuL-6 (20.2 mF cm−2) and p-CuL-8 (4.6 mF cm−2), respectively. This result indicated the highest ESCA of p-CuL-4. Furthermore, p-CuL-4 also displayed the highest jacetate nor-
malized to ESCA at the same potential among the three catalysts (Fig. S5†).
Tafel plots of log jacetate as a function of the applied potential were measured to further study the CO2 activation and reduction on various p-CuL-t catalysts. In Fig. 4E, the plots of p-CuL-4 and p-CuL-6 demonstrated approximately similar slopes of 92.4 and 95 mV dec−1, respectively, while p-CuL-8 showed the highest value of 118.4 mV dec−1. These values demonstrated that the single electron transfer to CO2 to form the adsorbed CO2
•− anion radical was likely the rate-determining step in the CO2RR on all p-CuL catalysts
41,42 and that p-CuL-8 exhibited the largest kinetic limitation. These analyses from a kinetic viewpoint indicated that the 3D porous framework of p-CuL-4 was the most favourable for the electron transfer and mass transport and thus had the highest electrocatalytic activity.
The durability of p-CuL as the working electrode was investigated by its repeated use for the CO2RR five times (1 h each time) and continuous monitoring of the current density at a constant potential. At a given potential of −0.37 V vs. RHE, the p-CuL electrode produced a constant current density; moreover, the acetate FE remained about 62 ± 2% as shown in Fig. 4F, confirming the good stability of p-CuL in the CO2 electrocatalytic reduction. In addition, the leaching of copper content was tested in a continuous CO2RR. The ICP results showed little change of the copper content in the electrolyte solution after the CO2RR for 1 and 2 h (0.10 and 0.096 mg, respectively). The small amount of leached Cu probably origi-

To understand the high product selectivity and considerable FEacetate from the CO2RR on the porous p-CuL, ex situ soft XAS was used to probe the electronic structure and local coordination environment.43,44 Taking the Cu(II)–urea precursor as a reference, Cu LIII-edge XAS spectra provided direct information about the chemical state and Cu–ligand strength of p-CuL before and after the electrocatalytic CO2RR. As shown in Fig. 5A, the excitation energy of the CuLIII peak of p-CuL shifted up to 931.0 eV, relative to that of Cu–OvC coordination dominant in the Cu(II)–urea precursor (930.5 eV), as a consequence of the incorporation of Cu–N due to the N-donor having stronger ligand-field strength than the O-donor.45 After the CO2RR, a noticeable extra peak appeared at 934.8 eV, corresponding to the Cu(I)–ligand complex, which was slightly higher than the photon energy of the Cu(I)–O bond (933.6 eV).46,47 The weakening Cu LIII peak at 930.5 eV was probably attributed to residual copper coordination similar to the Cu– urea precursor in p-CuL. This result revealed that Cuδ+ sites cocoordinated with N and carbonyl groups were markedly reduced to Cu(I), while Cu(II)–OvC coordination was very stable in the electrocatalytic CO2RR. Thus Cu
δ+–L (L = carbonyl group and N) coordination in p-CuL was likely the active site for the CO2RR to form acetate.
Furthermore, the electron transition from the ligand to the metal was confirmed by the N K-edge absorption spectra. In reference to the Cu–urea precursor, two π* peaks at 399.4 eV and 400.8 eV and a board σ* peak near 407 eV were assignable to pyridinic N, pyrrolic N and C–N bonding in the p-CuL catalyst (Fig. 5B), respectively. After the CO2RR, the π* transition
(pyridinic N) shifted 0.4 eV to higher energy and the intensity of the pyrrole peak slightly increased (dashed boxes). This suggested charge transfer from pyridinic as well as pyrrolic N to coordinated copper atoms in the electrocatalytic reduction process.45,48,49 The remarkable increase of the peak intensity in the O K-edge spectra revealed the increased surface oxygencontaining groups in the CO2RR. As seen from Fig. 5C, in the pre-edge 1s–π* transition region, a strong feature at 532 eV and the new π* transition at 534.5 eV assigned to the CvO group and –OH in carbonyl groups were dramatically enhanced50 on the p-CuL catalyst after the electrocatalytic CO2RR. This indirectly evidenced that the local environment of the Cuδ+– ligand sites with N and carbonyl groups was preferable for the adsorption of some important intermediates, e.g., *CO or *COOH. Based on the above analysis, the electrocatalytic CO2RR process and a possible acetate formation mechanism on p-CuL are displayed in Fig. 5D. Though the C–C coupling was still under debate, the synergy of two adjacent active sites was necessary.18,20 In our case, the high selectivity of acetate formation on p-CuL was considered to be related to the Cu(I)– N coordination. The single-electron reduction of CO2 molecules adsorbed on Cu(I) and N sites produced CO2 •− radical anions in the first step. After further e−/H+ transfer, the adsorbed CO2
•− was reduced to adsorbed *CO. Due to the stronger adsorption capacity of Cu sites towards CO in comparison to N sites, CO likely desorbed from N sites and transferred to Cu sites to couple with the adsorbed active *CH3,
21 thus resulting in the C–C dimerization. Further reduction of acetaldehyde produced the final acetate product.20,51

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
In summary, highly selective electrochemical reduction of CO2 to acetate is reported with a new polymeric Cu–L (L = pyridinic N and carbonyl group) complex core–shell microsphere catalyst. The catalyst is synthesized by the thermal-polymerization of a Cu–urea complex and urea, and its morphology can be tailored by controlling the reaction time. This catalyst features a unique co-coordination of pyridinic N and carbonyl groups with copper (mixed chemical state). The porous 3D core benefits the electron transfer and mass transport to enhance the faradaic efficiency. A large FEacetate of 64% is obtained at −0.37 V vs. RHE and is stable over cyclic tests. Ex situ XAS results suggest that Cuδ+ is likely reduced to Cu(I) in the CO2RR, and the unique coordination environment of Cu δ+– ligand active sites is probably preferable for the adsorption of some important intermediates, e.g. *CO or *COOH, to benefit the selective formation of acetate.
